newsitem.title: CANADA: US oil merger talk "wake up call" for Canada firms.
newsitem.headline: US oil merger talk "wake up call" for Canada firms.

text.p: A huge downstream oil merger being discussed by energy giants in the U.S. may cause hard-pressed Canadian refiners to take hard looks at their own operations, industry experts said on Monday.

Analysts have already served investors notice that Canada's integrated oil companies face dismal third-quarter returns after three months of extremely high crude oil costs and eastern Canadian retail gasoline price wars.

"In refining and marketing you either have to go really big or you've got to stay home," said Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp. "And with what happens in the third quarter, everybody's got to take a look at this business because they're not even making returns on their cost of capital."

Shell Oil Co, Texaco Inc and Saudi Arabia's Aramco confirmed on Monday they were in talks aimed at merging their U.S. refining and marketing businesses in a deal that would see US$10 billion of assets operated under one umbrella.
The talks were progressing after years of failed efforts to improve downstream returns in the United States.
In Canada, despite the closure of several refineries and thousands of service stations in the last five years, refining and marketing margins have remained razor thin.

Canadian integrateds "are going to have to look at every angle, expecially since they're all going to get obliterated in the third quarter," Molyneaux said, adding that the potential merger in the United States was a "big-time wake up call" for companies north of the border.
Canada's three national refiner/marketers are Imperial Oil Ltd, Shell Canada Ltd and Petro-Canada. Shell Canada said on Monday it was not involved in the U.S. merger.
Large regional refiners and marketers include Suncor Inc and Ultramar Corp in eastern Canada and Chevron Corp and Husky Oil Ltd in the west.

Most moves over the past five years to gain competitiveness in the country's downstream sector have come from within various companies and involved boosting refinery usage into the 90-percent range and station throughput.

"Companies have been consolidating (their own operations) and looking at the levers of technology and other costs to make themselves as much as they can to be lowest-cost refiner," said Petro-Canada spokesman Bill Simpkins.
Simpkins said he had not heard of any impending Canadian downstream mergers, at least involving Petro-Canada.

Ken Croft, analyst with Levesque Beaubien Geoffrion, said also, that because Canada was left with only three national marketers after Petro-Canada's takeover of Gulf Canada downstream assets and Imperial's acquisition of Texaco's refining and marketing business in the late 1980s, the odds of a megamerger appeared thin.
Croft said Canada's Bureau of Competition Policy would put any such merger under onerous scrutiny.
"The anti-trust guys are doing nothing, and any proposed merger between a couple of the majors would obviously raise flags," he said.

Also, despite thin margins, competition in Canada is not as brisk as in the United States because there are far fewer firms in the market that are pure refiners and marketers. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
